title: Every employee with their department
text: List every employee with the department they belong to. Return `name` and `department`, one row per employee.
answer:
### Approach
Each employee row carries a `department_id`; join it to `department` on the key and read the name from the other side. An inner join is the right default here, since every employee in the data has a department.

### Clause by clause
- `FROM employee e JOIN department d ON d.id = e.department_id` pairs each employee with exactly one department, because `d.id` is the primary key.
- `e.name AS name, d.name AS department`: both tables have a column called `name`. Without the aliases the result has two columns with the same name, and the second one does not say what it is.

### Edge cases
- An employee whose `department_id` is NULL, or points at a missing department, would vanish from an inner join. None does here. If the prompt said "every employee, even without a department", the fix is `LEFT JOIN`, and the department would come back NULL.
- Research has no employees, so it appears nowhere. That is correct: the question is one row per employee, not per department.
- Row order is not checked, so no ORDER BY is needed.

guides.title: Joins that keep the right rows
